title: “Drums”: The Piano as Percussion Ensemble in Prelude and Fugue No.3, Book II
content_blocks: This pair of pieces explores the percussive potential of the prepared piano:  using a variety of materials, the pitched quality of ordinary piano sounds can be suppressed, turning the piano into a collection of graduated toms, bass and snare-like drums, along with tambourine-like drums with bangles.  In the videos linked to below, you can see the sponges and boxes of cards that I used on the lowest strings, and just a few of the erasers that I used on the higher strings (they’re hard to see).  You can also see some of the bangles that are positioned in a variety of ways—yes, I had fun experimenting!

The prelude is built around the idea of a “Risset Clock”—essentially the temporal equivalent of a barbershop pole, where as a figure speeds up, it reappears simultaneously at a slower rate, giving the illusion of always accelerating.  Since there are as many as three different “stripes” of the accelerating barbershop pole heard at once, in effect this Risset Clock is really another type of fugue!

The fugue itself is a straightforward four-part “percussion ensemble” fugue, with the voices very clearly arranged from lowest up to highest. Each voice’s subject (main figure) and subsequent countersubject (what is heard when the next voice enters) ends with a tambourine hit. These punctuations do not necessarily mark the end of a section, although the end of all of the sections are marked by a tambourine hit.

Recording these pieces with Mika was also quite fun. She had practiced on the piano, but since the preparations remove almost all traces of actual pitch, the sound in the recording session was completely different from what she had been hearing. One little joke that even Mika may not have been aware of: Each prelude and fugue pair in both books is said to be in a specific “key.” In the first book, those pitches are clear, but the keys are often not so clear, since they are mostly in newly-created modes. In the second book, some of the pitches and keys are quite clear (especially in the last five pairs), but in this pair there is no discernible pitch. Nevertheless, I describe the piece as being “in B,” since the piano strings used the most are Bs. Perhaps that explains Mika’s quizzical expression at the end of the recording of both the Prelude and the Fugue!
In the videos linked to below, you can see the sponges and boxes of cards that I used on the lowest strings, and just a few of the erasers that I used on the higher strings.
